blocks.title: Thermistor
blocks.text: A thermistor is a heat-sensitive resistor. Most thermistors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance, that is, their resistance decreases when their temperature is increased; thermistors with a positive temperature coefficient are also available.

In thermistors the resistance decreases as the temperature increases because the increasing temperature provides more energy to the charge carriers (electrons or holes), enabling them to move more freely and thus reducing the resistance. Thermistors are made by heating, under high pressure, a semiconductor ceramic made from mixtures of metallic oxides of manganese, nickel, cobalt, copper, iron and so on. These are pressed into the desired shapes and then baked at high temperature; they may be in the form of beads, rods or washers (Figs. 9.33, thermistor symbols, and 9.34, types of thermistors).

blocks.alt: Two thermistor symbols. (a) A resistor zigzag inside a circle with a slanting arrow across it. (b) A resistor rectangle with a slanting line with a short flat foot, meaning the resistance changes with temperature.
blocks.caption: Thermistor symbols (original diagram after Figure 9.33).

items: Temperature measurement: thermistors are used in thermometers and in electric devices such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heaters, microwave ovens and incubators to monitor temperature. Thermistors with a high negative temperature coefficient are very accurate for measuring low temperatures, especially near 10 K, where their higher resistance makes more accurate measurement possible. As temperature sensors they convert changes of temperature into an electrical voltage, which is duly processed; for example, they are used in coolant temperature sensors in automobile engines to prevent overheating, and in digital thermometers.
Temperature compensation: thermistors are used in circuits where temperature changes could affect performance, such as oscillators, battery charging circuits and power systems.
Inrush current limiting: thermistors are used to limit the initial flow of current when a device is first turned on.

Voltage divider: thermistors are widely used in voltage dividers (Fig. 9.35). When the temperature of the thermistor increases its resistance decreases, which decreases the voltage drop across it. This change in the potential at point B can be used to trigger a circuit connected to it. In a fire alarm, the heated thermistor turns the input of a NOT gate low; the output of the NOT gate goes high and turns the siren on.

blocks.alt: A battery across a fixed resistor in series with a thermistor; point B between them feeds a NOT gate that drives a siren. A note says heat lowers the thermistor's resistance, so the voltage across it at B falls; the NOT gate's input goes low, its output goes high and the siren sounds.
